blueprint.title: Log Aggregator Rollup Drift
blueprint.scenario: You maintain a backend service that ingests structured JSON access logs from a running web app, aggregates them into per-minute rollup records stored in SQLite, and exposes a summary endpoint. The aggregation daemon is a compiled C binary (/usr/local/bin/logroll) with no source available. Since a recent deploy, downstream dashboards show rollup counts drifting from raw log counts, but only under real traffic patterns — the synthetic smoke-test the team wrote always passes. There are about 1,400 lines of Python glue code, config files, and a live Nginx instance generating traffic inside the container.
blueprint.instruction_draft: Hey, the log rollup service is messed up again. The `/app/rollup/db/rollups.db` SQLite database should have one row per (minute_bucket, status_class) pair where `count` equals the exact number of raw log lines in `/app/logs/access.log` that fall in that bucket and class. Same for `bytes_sum` — it should equal the sum of `response_bytes` for those lines. Right now the numbers are wrong under real traffic. Also, we recently added a new feature: the rollup service needs to write a companion file `/app/rollup/db/anomalies.json` that lists every minute_bucket where any status_class had a count spike — meaning its count is more than 2 standard deviations above that status_class's mean count across all buckets. Each entry should be `{"bucket": "...", "status_class": "...", "count": N}`. That file doesn't exist yet, you'll need to build it. Make sure both the db rows and the anomalies file are correct after you run whatever pipeline you put together.
requirements: For every (minute_bucket, status_class) pair present in /app/logs/access.log, the rollups.db table `rollups` must have a row where `count` equals the exact number of matching log lines.
For every such pair, `bytes_sum` must equal the exact sum of `response_bytes` for matching log lines.
The file /app/rollup/db/anomalies.json must exist and be valid JSON.
anomalies.json must contain exactly the set of (bucket, status_class) entries where count > mean + 2*stddev for that status_class across all buckets.
Each anomaly entry must have keys: bucket (string, format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM), status_class (string e.g. '2xx'), count (integer).
No spurious entries may appear in anomalies.json — only genuine spikes qualify.
environment: Install: sqlite3, nginx, gcc, python3 packages (flask, schedule, watchdog), all pinned.

Compile and install /usr/local/bin/logroll from a C source that is NOT left on disk. The binary reads a JSON log file path as argv[1] and a SQLite db path as argv[2], upserts rollup rows into table `rollups(minute_bucket TEXT, status_class TEXT, count INTEGER, bytes_sum INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY(minute_bucket, status_class))`. The binary has a deliberate bug: it truncates response_bytes values to uint16 (max 65535) before summing, so bytes_sum is wrong for large responses. It also silently drops log lines whose `ts` field is not in ISO-8601 format (a format the real log generator sometimes emits for high-load bursts — a unix-epoch integer string). Neither bug is visible without running it on realistic data.

A Python log generator script /app/loggen/generator.py runs as a background service (systemd-style via a supervisor or simple loop). It writes JSON lines to /app/logs/access.log. ~80% of lines have ISO-8601 ts, ~20% have unix-epoch integer ts. response_bytes are drawn from a distribution where ~5% exceed 65535. This creates both the ts-drop bug and the bytes truncation bug.
A Python orchestrator /app/rollup/orchestrator.py calls logroll periodically (every 30s) and is the glue code the solver will read. It does NOT implement anomaly detection — that's the new feature.

About 800 lines of additional Python across /app/rollup/ covering config parsing, health endpoints (Flask), a metrics exporter, a log rotation helper, and unit tests for the smoke-test suite. None of this code contains the bug.
Nginx runs and generates synthetic traffic to a stub endpoint, with access logged to /app/logs/access.log via a Python middleware that formats lines. The middleware is in /app/loggen/ (~200 lines).
The smoke-test at /app/tests/smoke_test.py generates only ISO-8601 timestamps and response_bytes < 65535, so it always passes against the buggy binary.
Provide /app/README.md describing the rollup schema and the anomaly file format.
Pre-populate /app/logs/access.log with ~5000 realistic lines (seeded) so the bugs are already manifested in the db before the solver starts.
The rollups.db is pre-populated by running logroll on the existing log, so it already contains wrong data.
A seed-based script /app/scripts/gen_verify_log.py is used at verify time to generate a fresh deterministic log and check the solver's pipeline against it.
blueprint.internal_hint: Difficulty comes from two opaque_component bugs in the compiled logroll binary that are invisible by source inspection: (1) unix-epoch ts lines are silently dropped (observe_not_read: only ~20% of lines, only visible when running on real data), and (2) response_bytes are truncated to uint16 before summing (only affects ~5% of lines). The solver must characterize the binary by experiment — feed it controlled inputs and diff against ground truth — to discover both bugs. The fix is to bypass logroll entirely and reimplement the aggregation in Python (or any language), reading the raw log correctly. The new feature (anomalies.json) requires correctly aggregating first, then computing per-status_class mean and stddev, which is straightforward once the aggregation is correct. A solver who patches only the ts bug will still fail bytes_sum checks. A solver who fixes aggregation but computes anomalies from the still-wrong db will produce wrong anomaly entries.
blueprint.trap: A naive solver runs logroll on the existing log, sees that most counts look plausible (80% of lines land correctly), and writes the anomaly detector on top of the still-wrong db. The hidden verifier uses a fresh log with different seeds where the spike pattern is different, and also checks bytes_sum precisely — which logroll always gets wrong for large-response lines. The solver also fails if they only fix the ts format issue but keep using logroll (bytes_sum still truncated). Shallow verification against the provided sample passes because the smoke test was designed to avoid both bugs.
tests: At verify time, /app/scripts/gen_verify_log.py generates a fresh deterministic access.log (different seed) with ~3000 lines including ~20% unix-epoch ts and ~6% large-response lines, writes it to a temp path, then runs the solver's pipeline against it.
Test 1: Query rollups.db for all rows; compare count per (bucket, status_class) against ground truth computed directly from the raw log lines in Python. All must match exactly.
Test 2: Query rollups.db for bytes_sum per (bucket, status_class); compare against Python ground truth sum of response_bytes (full integer, no truncation). All must match exactly.

Test 3: Parse /app/rollup/db/anomalies.json; verify it is valid JSON and contains exactly the entries where count > mean(status_class) + 2*std(status_class) across all buckets (computed from ground truth counts). No missing, no spurious entries.
Test 4: Verify each anomaly entry has exactly the keys bucket, status_class, count with correct types and values.
Test 5: Re-run the solver's pipeline on a second fresh log (seed+1) to verify the pipeline is general, not hardcoded to the original data.

verifier_knob.name: number_of_independent_state_properties_checked
verifier_knob.value: 5 (count correctness, bytes_sum correctness, anomalies.json existence+validity, anomaly set correctness, anomaly entry schema)
verifier_knob.effect: Dropping bytes_sum check makes it easier (solver only needs to fix ts bug); adding a third fresh-log replay or checking rollup completeness for zero-count buckets makes it harder.

expected_failure_modes: Solver fixes the ts format bug by preprocessing the log before passing to logroll, but keeps logroll for bytes_sum — bytes_sum tests still fail because of uint16 truncation.
Solver replaces logroll correctly but builds anomaly detection on the old (wrong) rollups.db rows rather than recomputing from scratch, producing wrong anomaly counts.

Solver writes anomaly detection that computes stddev incorrectly (e.g., population vs sample, or wrong mean scope — per bucket vs per status_class), passes on the provided sample but fails on the verify-time log where spike distribution differs.
Solver characterizes only one of the two binary bugs (ts drop OR bytes truncation) via limited experiments and considers the binary fixed after patching one issue.
Solver hardcodes anomaly thresholds from the existing data rather than computing dynamically, fails on fresh verify-time log.

# Both bugs confirmed. Write replacement aggregation in Python.

cat > /app/rollup/aggregate.py << 'EOF'
import json, sqlite3, sys, datetime, collections, math, os

LOG_PATH = '/app/logs/access.log'
DB_PATH = '/app/rollup/db/rollups.db'
ANOM_PATH = '/app/rollup/db/anomalies.json'

def parse_ts(ts):
    if isinstance(ts, int) or (isinstance(ts, str) and ts.isdigit()):
        return datetime.datetime.utcfromtimestamp(int(ts))
    return datetime.datetime.fromisoformat(ts.replace('Z',''))

def status_class(code):
    return f"{code//100}xx"

lines = [json.loads(l) for l in open(LOG_PATH)]
buckets = collections.defaultdict(lambda: {'count':0,'bytes_sum':0})
for l in lines:
    dt = parse_ts(l['ts'])
    bucket = dt.strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M')
    sc = status_class(int(l['status']))
    key = (bucket, sc)
    buckets[key]['count'] += 1
    buckets[key]['bytes_sum'] += int(l['response_bytes'])

con = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
con.execute('CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS rollups(minute_bucket TEXT, status_class TEXT, count INTEGER, bytes_sum INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY(minute_bucket, status_class))')
con.execute('DELETE FROM rollups')
for (mb, sc), v in buckets.items():
    con.execute('INSERT INTO rollups VALUES(?,?,?,?)', (mb, sc, v['count'], v['bytes_sum']))
con.commit()

# Anomaly detection
by_class = collections.defaultdict(list)
for (mb, sc), v in buckets.items():
    by_class[sc].append((mb, v['count']))

anomalies = []
for sc, entries in by_class.items():
    counts = [e[1] for e in entries]
    mean = sum(counts)/len(counts)
    std = math.sqrt(sum((c-mean)**2 for c in counts)/len(counts))
    threshold = mean + 2*std
    for mb, cnt in entries:
        if cnt > threshold:
            anomalies.append({'bucket': mb, 'status_class': sc, 'count': cnt})

with open(ANOM_PATH, 'w') as f:
    json.dump(anomalies, f)
print(f'Done: {len(buckets)} rollup rows, {len(anomalies)} anomalies')
EOF

invalid_failure_risks: Population vs sample stddev ambiguity: the instruction says '2 standard deviations above the mean' without specifying population vs sample stddev. The verifier must use the same convention as the instruction implies; if the verifier uses sample stddev (ddof=1) but a solver uses population stddev (ddof=0), borderline spikes could differ, causing a false failure on valid solutions.

The verify-time script gen_verify_log.py writes to a temp path and 'runs the solver's pipeline against it' — but the solver's pipeline (aggregate.py) hardcodes LOG_PATH='/app/logs/access.log'. The verifier must either swap the log file or pass a path argument; if the interface contract isn't clear, a correct general solution could fail because it reads the wrong file.

Timing/race condition: if the log generator (background service) is still writing to access.log during verification, the ground truth computed by the verifier and the data read by the solver's pipeline could differ, causing flaky count mismatches.

The instruction says 'run whatever pipeline you put together' but doesn't specify how the verifier invokes the solver's pipeline — if it expects a specific entry point (e.g., python3 /app/rollup/aggregate.py) vs. a shell script, a solver who names their script differently could fail for non-substantive reasons.

The anomaly format example shows 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM' for bucket but the log ts parsing could produce UTC vs local time differences depending on the container timezone, causing bucket mismatches between solver and verifier ground truth.
review.reasons: The task scores well across all dimensions: it presents a realistic ops scenario with two genuinely hidden bugs in an opaque binary that require experimental characterization, not source reading. The speedrun reaches ~17 commands but requires non-trivial experimental steps (feeding controlled inputs to logroll to discover both the uint16 truncation and the ts-drop bugs) that a shallow agent would skip, making genuine failure likely. The verifier uses a fresh deterministic log, preventing hardcoding, and checks 5 independent properties. The main risks are the stddev convention ambiguity and the pipeline invocation interface, which should be tightened.
fixes: Explicitly specify population stddev (ddof=0) vs sample stddev (ddof=1) in the anomaly detection requirement to eliminate borderline-case disagreements between solver and verifier.

Define a clear pipeline entry point contract (e.g., 'your solution must be invocable as `python3 /app/rollup/pipeline.py <log_path> <db_path>`') so the verifier can substitute the fresh log path without the solver hardcoding paths.

Stop the log generator background service before verification begins (or document that verification freezes the log) to eliminate race conditions between the live writer and the verifier's ground-truth computation.
Add a note in the README or instruction that the container timezone is UTC, to prevent ts-parsing timezone ambiguity in bucket assignment.

verdicts.reason: That task is about detecting network attack patterns in traffic logs via shell scripting; this task is about fixing SQLite rollup aggregation drift and building an anomaly detection file from web access logs.

Both tasks involve a compiled binary with no source, SQLite rollup tables that produce wrong aggregated values under real data, and require the agent to characterize/bypass the binary and fix downstream correctness — the core challenge and approach are essentially the same, even though the domain (IoT sensors vs. web access logs) and specific output artifacts differ.
That task is a straightforward log-parsing and CSV-writing exercise with no broken pipeline, no compiled binary, and no database rollup repair.

That task involves fixing source code in a sales aggregation service and rebuilding a binary; this task involves a black-box compiled binary, log parsing, SQLite rollup drift, and anomaly detection file generation.
That task is about fixing a Node.js NDJSON validation pipeline for correctness and performance; this task is about SQLite rollup drift from a compiled binary and anomaly detection.
